mainTopic: צדקה: how much a poor person must be given (דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ), how to help someone who refuses, and giving without causing shame
overview: The amud opens by finishing a rule: when an orphan girl and an orphan boy both need help marrying, the girl comes first. Two ברייתות then read the פסוק 'דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ אֲשֶׁר יֶחְסַר לוֹ'. You must give a poor person what he is missing, but you do not have to make him rich. For someone used to luxury, what he is missing can even include a horse and a servant. Stories about הלל הזקן, the people of the Upper גליל, רבי נחמיה and רבא show how far this goes, and also the danger of getting too used to luxury. Next the גמרא discusses how to help a poor man who refuses צדקה, and a man who has money but will not spend it. Here רבי מאיר, חכמים, רבי שמעון and רבי יהודה each give a view, and רבי יהודה reads the double wording 'הַעֲבֵט תַּעֲבִיטֶנּוּ' as two cases. The amud ends with stories about giving with dignity. In one, מר עוקבא and his wife hide in a hot furnace, because it is better to be burned than to shame someone in public, as we learn from תמר. In others, מר עוקבא gives away half his money as he is dying, which is allowed despite the one-fifth limit, and רבי אבא gives in a hidden way. The story of רבי חנינא's wife begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Orphan girl is married off before orphan boy
steps.stepSummary: When an orphan boy and girl both ask the צדקה fund for help marrying, the girl is helped first, because an unmarried woman suffers more embarrassment.
steps.simpleTranslation: [An orphan boy and orphan girl] who came to be married: we marry off the orphan girl first and then the orphan boy, because a woman's embarrassment is greater than a man's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a rule that started on the previous page. It sets the order of priority between two orphans who need help getting married.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is based on בושה, embarrassment. Since an unmarried woman suffers more shame than an unmarried man, her need is more urgent, so she goes first.

keyTerms.meaning: They marry off (arrange and pay for the marriage)

phrases.english: who came to be married —
phrases.notes: This line continues from the previous page, which is talking about an orphan boy and an orphan girl who both need help.

phrases.english: they marry off the orphan girl
and afterward they marry off the orphan boy,
because the embarrassment of a woman
is greater than that of a man.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַשִּׂיאִין אֶת הַיְּתוֹמָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ מַשִּׂיאִין אֶת הַיָּתוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ברייתא that began on the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An orphan girl is married off before an orphan boy, because a woman's shame is greater.

steps.title: An orphan groom gets a house, furniture, then a wife
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that the community sets up an orphan groom with a rented house, bed and utensils, and then a wife. Each item is read into a part of the פסוק 'דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ אֲשֶׁר יֶחְסַר לוֹ'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: When an orphan comes to marry, they rent him a house, set up a bed and all his utensils, and then marry him to a wife. As it says, 'enough for his lack, which he lacks, for him.' 'Enough for his lack' is the house. 'Which he lacks' is a bed and table. 'For him' is a wife.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא teaches how fully the community provides for an orphan groom. It backs this up by splitting a פסוק into three parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has three phrases, and each one points to a different need: a house, furniture, and a wife. The order of the פסוק matches the order of the help. First a home is ready, and only then the marriage.

keyTerms.meaning: They set up or spread out (a bed)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key פסוק that the rest of the section uses to define how far צדקה must go.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
An orphan boy who comes to marry —
they rent a house for him,
and they set up a bed for him
and all his household utensils,
and afterward they marry him to a wife,
as it says: 'enough for his lack, which he lacks, for him.'
'Enough for his lack' — this is the house,
'which he lacks' — this is a bed and a table,
'for him' — this is a wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of helping orphans marry, now about what an orphan groom receives.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An orphan groom is given a rented house, a bed and utensils, and then a wife, learned from דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ אֲשֶׁר יֶחְסַר לוֹ.

steps.title: Proof that the word 'לוֹ' can mean a wife
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא supports reading 'לוֹ' as a wife by pointing to the פסוק about חוה, where 'לוֹ' also refers to a wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: 'I will make for him a helper opposite him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings support for its last reading, that the small word 'לוֹ' hints to a wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading 'for him' as a wife could seem like a stretch. So the ברייתא shows that the Torah uses the same word 'לוֹ' when ה׳ made a wife for אדם.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says (brings a supporting פסוק)

phrases.english: And so it says:
'I will make for him a helper opposite him.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 2:18. The same word 'לוֹ' appears here, and it is about a wife.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״אֶעֱשֶׂה לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reading of 'לוֹ' as a wife from step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That 'לוֹ' in דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ refers to a wife.

steps.title: Support him, not make him rich, but even a horse and servant
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא sets the limits of צדקה: you must cover what the poor person lacks but need not make him rich. Still, 'what he lacks' can include a horse and a servant for someone used to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'Enough for his lack': you are commanded to support him, but you are not commanded to make him rich. 'Which he lacks for him': even a horse to ride on and a servant to run before him.
steps.whatsHappening: A second ברייתא reads the same פסוק to show both the limit and the reach of the מצוה of צדקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ' limits the duty to filling what is missing, not adding wealth. 'אֲשֶׁר יֶחְסַר לוֹ' measures that lack by what this particular person is used to. So a horse and a servant are not luxury for a formerly rich man; they are part of what he is missing.

keyTerms.meaning: To support him (give him what he needs)
To run in front of him (an honor guard)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a contradiction. Both rules measure the same thing: what this person lacks. Making him rich is not required, but giving back the standard he lost is.
steps.whatToRemember: צדקה fills what a person is missing, judged by what he was used to. It does not have to make him rich.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'Enough for his lack' —
you are commanded regarding him to support him,
but you are not commanded regarding him to make him rich.
'Which he lacks for him' —
even a horse to ride on
and a servant to run in front of him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״דֵּי מַחְסוֹרוֹ״ — אַתָּה מְצֻוֶּוה עָלָיו לְפַרְנְסוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same פסוק from step 2 to define the limits of צדקה in general.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You must support a poor person but not make him rich, and 'his lack' can include a horse and servant if he was used to them.

steps.title: הלל הזקן runs before a poor man
steps.stepSummary: A story: הלל הזקן provided a horse and servant for a formerly wealthy poor man, and once, when no servant was available, ran before him himself for three מילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said about הלל הזקן that he got a poor man from a good family a horse to ride on and a servant to run before him. Once he could not find a servant, so he himself ran before him for three מילין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the rule of step 4 in action.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story shows that the horse-and-servant rule was really practiced. הלל went even further: when he could not hire a servant, he filled that missing role with his own body.

keyTerms.meaning: A poor man from a well-off family (who became poor)
Mil, a unit of distance (roughly a kilometer)

phrases.english: They said about הלל the Elder
that he got for a certain poor man from a good family

phrases.aramaic: סוּס לִרְכּוֹב עָלָיו וְעֶבֶד לָרוּץ לְפָנָיו.
phrases.english: a horse to ride on and a servant to run in front of him.

phrases.aramaic: פַּעַם אַחַת לֹא מָצָא עֶבֶד לָרוּץ לְפָנָיו,
phrases.english: One time he did not find a servant to run in front of him,
so he ran in front of him for three mil.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule of step 4 being carried out.
steps.raayaObject: That 'אֲשֶׁר יֶחְסַר לוֹ' includes a horse and a servant for a formerly wealthy person.

steps.title: The people of the Upper גליל buy daily meat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells that the people of the Upper גליל bought a ליטרא of meat every day for a formerly wealthy poor man from ציפורי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: There was a story with the people of the Upper Galilee, who bought a ליטרא of meat every day for a poor man from a good family from ציפורי.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story about supporting a formerly wealthy poor man. It sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the הלל story, this shows a community giving a poor man the standard he was used to. But as told, the gift does not sound unusual, which leads into the גמרא's question.

keyTerms.meaning: ציפורי, a town in the Galilee
A ליטרא, a unit of weight (about a pound)

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאַנְשֵׁי גָּלִיל הָעֶלְיוֹן
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: There was a story with the people of the Upper Galilee

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלָּקְחוּ לְעָנִי בֶּן טוֹבִים אֶחָד מִצִּיפּוֹרִי
phrases.english: who bought for a certain poor man from a good family, from ציפורי,
a litra of meat every day.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאַנְשֵׁי גָּלִיל הָעֶלְיוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story on the same theme as the הלל story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The community bought a formerly wealthy poor man a ליטרא of meat daily.

steps.title: What is so special about a pound of meat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why this story is worth telling, since a ליטרא of meat a day does not sound like a big deal.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ליטרא of meat: what is the big deal?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the story. It sets up three answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A story is only kept if it teaches something. A normal amount of meat would not show special effort, so the גמרא asks what made this gift unusual.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the big deal? What is new here?

phrases.english: A litra of meat — what is the big deal?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the point of the story in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What made a daily ליטרא of meat special enough to record.

steps.title: רב הונא: It was expensive poultry
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers that the ליטרא was of poultry, which is costly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: A ליטרא of poultry meat.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives the first answer to the question: the meat was fowl, not regular meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Poultry was expensive, so a pound of it every day was a big cost. That is the special effort the story shows.

phrases.english: רב הונא said:
A litra of meat from poultry.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: לִיטְרָא בָּשָׂר מִשֶּׁל עוֹפוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The meat was poultry, which is very expensive.

steps.title: Second answer: regular meat bought for a ליטרא of coins
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: read it as 'for a ליטרא'. They paid a ליטרא of money for ordinary meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: for a ליטרא they bought actual meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to answer the question by reading the words differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'ליטרא' is not the weight of the meat but the amount of money paid. Ordinary meat was so costly there that it cost a ליטרא of coins each day.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
for a litra, they bought actual meat.
phrases.notes: Here the ליטרא is the money they paid, not how much the meat weighed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the question of step 7, instead of רב הונא's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They spent a ליטרא of coins each day on ordinary meat.

steps.title: רב אשי: A whole animal was wasted for him daily
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the village was small, so they had to slaughter an animal every day just for this one man, and the rest went to waste.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: There it was a small village, and every day they lost an animal because of him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third answer to the question: the cost was not the price but the waste.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a small village nobody else would buy the rest of the meat. So to give him fresh meat every day, they slaughtered a whole animal and lost most of it. That loss is what made the gift remarkable.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of him, for his sake

steps.whatToRemember: Three answers for why the meat was special: it was poultry (רב הונא), it cost a ליטרא of coins, or a whole animal was wasted daily (רב אשי). All three show the community paid a high cost to keep his old standard.

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
There it was a small village,

phrases.aramaic: בְּכׇל יוֹמָא הֲוָה מַפְסְדִי חֵיוְתָא אַמְּטוּלְתֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: and every day they would lose an animal because of him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: הָתָם כְּפָר קָטָן הָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In a small village a whole animal had to be slaughtered daily just for him, and the rest was wasted.

steps.title: A spoiled poor man eats lentils with רבי נחמיה and dies
steps.stepSummary: A poor man used to fatty meat and aged wine eats simple lentils with רבי נחמיה and dies. רבי נחמיה cries out, 'Woe to this one whom נחמיה killed.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A man came to רבי נחמיה for help. רבי נחמיה asked what he usually ate, and he said fatty meat and aged wine. רבי נחמיה asked him to share a simple meal of lentils. The man ate the lentils and died. רבי נחמיה said: Woe to this one whom נחמיה killed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about a poor man who was used to very rich food. It ends with a strange statement by רבי נחמיה that the גמרא will question next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story is the opposite of the earlier stories, where people worked hard to give a poor man the fancy food he was used to. Here רבי נחמיה offers only his own simple food, and the result is deadly. The wording of רבי נחמיה's cry, 'woe to this one,' sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: that you will 'roll along' with me, meaning lower yourself to share my simple meal

phrases.english: A certain man who came before Rabbi Nechemya,
he said to him: What do you usually dine on?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ בְּבָשָׂר שָׁמֵן וְיַיִן יָשָׁן.
phrases.english: He said to him: On fatty meat and aged wine.
Would you agree to lower yourself and share lentils with me?
He shared the lentils with him, and he died.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: אוֹי לוֹ לְזֶה שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ נְחֶמְיָה.
phrases.english: He said: Woe to this one whom Nechemya killed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story on the same theme as the ליטרא of meat story: what happens when a formerly wealthy poor man does not get the food he is used to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A formerly wealthy man ate the simple lentils of רבי נחמיה and died, and רבי נחמיה said 'woe to this one whom נחמיה killed.'

steps.title: Shouldn't he have said 'Woe to נחמיה'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי נחמיה's wording. If he caused the death, he should have said 'Woe to נחמיה who killed this man.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Just the opposite! He should have said: Woe to נחמיה who killed this man!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of רבי נחמיה's cry. It seems backwards, because the one who caused a death is the one who should be pitied for his guilt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Woe to this one' sounds like pity for the dead man. But if רבי נחמיה felt guilty, the natural wording would be 'woe to נחמיה,' blaming himself. The גמרא wants to know why he worded it this way.

keyTerms.meaning: on the contrary, just the opposite

phrases.english: On the contrary,

phrases.aramaic: ״אוֹי לוֹ לִנְחֶמְיָה שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ לְזֶה״ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ!
phrases.english: he should have said: 'Woe to Nechemya who killed this one'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of רבי נחמיה's statement in the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי נחמיה's words 'אוי לו לזה שהרגו נחמיה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The one who caused the death should be the one described as unfortunate, so the wording seems reversed.

steps.title: The poor man was to blame for spoiling himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי נחמיה meant the poor man himself was at fault. He should not have pampered himself so much that he could not handle simple food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he meant: it was the poor man himself who should not have pampered himself so much.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רבי נחמיה's wording was on purpose, because the blame really belongs to the poor man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man had spoiled himself with luxury until his body could not handle plain food. So the death came from his own choices, not from רבי נחמיה. 'Woe to this one' means 'woe to him for bringing this on himself.'

keyTerms.meaning: so much, to such a degree

steps.whatToRemember: The story of רבי נחמיה teaches that a person should not get too used to luxury, even when he can afford it.

phrases.english: Rather: it was he himself
phrases.notes: 'He' is the poor man, not רבי נחמיה.

phrases.english: who should not have
pampered himself so much.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: אִיהוּ הוּא דְּלָא אִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְפַנּוֹקֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ כּוּלֵּי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by moving the blame from רבי נחמיה to the poor man.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the intent of the statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי נחמיה's wording seemed backwards, since he appeared to be the one at fault.
steps.terutzMaskana: The poor man was at fault for over-pampering himself, so 'woe to this one' fits.

steps.title: A poor man asks רבא for fattened hen and aged wine
steps.stepSummary: A poor man tells רבא he eats fattened hen and aged wine. רבא asks if he is not worried about burdening the community. The man answers that he eats from הקב״ה, not from them.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man came to רבא for help. רבא asked what he usually ate. He said fattened hen and aged wine. רבא said: Aren't you worried about the burden you put on the community? He answered: Am I eating from their food? I am eating from the food of the Merciful One!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story, this time with רבא. The poor man defends his costly diet with a bold claim that the next step will back up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's concern is that the community's charity funds are limited. Spending them on luxury for one man hurts others. The man argues that the community is only passing along what הקב״ה gives him, so his food really comes from Heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: a fattened hen, a costly food
the burden or pressure on the community
is that to say? (a question that rejects the idea)

phrases.english: A certain man who came before Rava,
he said to him: What do you usually dine on?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: בְּתַרְנְגוֹלֶת פְּטוּמָה וְיַיִן יָשָׁן.
phrases.english: He said to him: On fattened hen and aged wine.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְלָא חָיְישַׁתְּ לְדוּחְקָא דְּצִיבּוּרָא?
phrases.english: He said to him: And are you not worried about the burden on the community?
He said to him: Is it from theirs that I eat?
I eat from the Merciful One's!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story with a different angle: here the poor man argues that his costly needs are justified.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The poor man claims his food comes from הקב״ה, not from the community, so his costly diet is no real burden on them.

steps.title: Proof from the פסוק: each person gets food 'in its time'
steps.stepSummary: The man's claim is backed up from the פסוק 'עיני כל אליך ישברו.' The singular 'בעתו' teaches that הקב״ה gives each individual his own food at his own time.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: 'The eyes of all wait for You, and You give them their food in its time.' It does not say 'in their time,' but 'in its time.' This teaches that הקב״ה gives each and every person his own sustenance at its time.
steps.whatsHappening: This step gives the proof for the poor man's claim. A precise reading of one word in a פסוק shows that each person gets his own food from הקב״ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק talks about 'all' in the plural, so we would expect 'בעתם,' 'their time.' Instead it says 'בעתו,' 'his time,' in the singular. This shows that הקב״ה sees to each person's individual needs, including someone used to fancy food.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read the proof as saying the poor man personally deserves luxury no matter what. The point is that each person's portion is set by הקב״ה, and the community is only the messenger who delivers it.

phrases.english: As we learned:
'The eyes of all wait for You,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַתָּה נוֹתֵן לָהֶם אֶת אׇכְלָם בְּעִתּוֹ״.
phrases.english: and You give them their food in its time.'
It does not say 'in their time,' but 'in its time' —
this teaches that to each and every one

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתֵן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא פַּרְנָסָתוֹ בְּעִתּוֹ.
phrases.english: the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives his sustenance in its time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the poor man's claim that he eats 'from the Merciful One.'
steps.raayaObject: The poor man's claim that his food comes from הקב״ה and fits his own needs

steps.title: רבא's sister arrives with the exact same food
steps.stepSummary: Just then רבא's sister, whom he had not seen for thirteen years, arrives with a fattened hen and aged wine. רבא sees it as a sign and tells the man: I give in to you, get up and eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile, רבא's sister, who had not seen him for thirteen years, arrived and brought him a fattened hen and aged wine. רבא said: What is this happening in front of me? He said to the man: I give in to you. Get up and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with a surprise that proves the poor man right. Heaven sends exactly the food he asked for, and רבא accepts his argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exact match between the gift and the man's request is a sign that הקב״ה provides each person his own portion. רבא drops his objection about burdening the community. The man's claim from step 15 is confirmed.

keyTerms.meaning: what is this in front of me?
I give in to you, I accept your argument

steps.whatToRemember: The two stories balance each other. A person should not spoil himself (רבי נחמיה), but a poor man used to more may be given according to his needs, since הקב״ה provides each person his own portion (רבא).

phrases.english: Meanwhile,
Rava's sister came,
who had not seen him for thirteen years,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַתְיָא לֵיהּ תַּרְנְגוֹלֶת פְּטוּמָה וְיַיִן יָשָׁן.
phrases.english: and she brought him a fattened hen and aged wine.
He said: What is this in front of me?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: נַעֲנֵתִי לְךָ, קוּם אֱכוֹל.
phrases.english: He said to him: I give in to you; get up and eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story by confirming the poor man's argument through a sign from Heaven.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבא accepts that the man's costly food is his portion from הקב״ה and invites him to eat.

steps.title: How to help a poor man who refuses צדקה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings a מחלוקת. רבי מאיר says to give it as a loan and then as a gift. חכמים say to give it as a gift and then as a loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If a person has nothing but does not want to be supported from צדקה, we give it to him as a loan, and then give it to him as a gift. This is the view of רבי מאיר. The חכמים say: We give it to him as a gift, and then give it to him as a loan.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a proud poor person who refuses help. רבי מאיר and חכמים argue about which way to offer it first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree we must find a respectful way to support him. רבי מאיר starts with a loan, which he can accept with dignity, and later it is treated as a gift. חכמים start by offering a gift and only then fall back on a loan.

keyTerms.meaning: and then they go back (and do the next thing)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If he has nothing and does not want to be supported —
we give it to him as a loan,
and then we go back and give it to him as a gift,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say:
we give it to him as a gift,
and then we go back and give it to him as a loan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from stories to a הלכה about giving צדקה with dignity.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: loan first, then gift. חכמים: gift first, then loan.

steps.title: How can it be a gift if he refuses to take it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the חכמים: how can we give him a gift? The whole case is that he refuses to take צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a gift? But he won't take it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view of חכמים. Offering a gift seems pointless when the case is about someone who refuses free help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is talking about a poor man who does not want to be supported. A gift is exactly what he is refusing. So the חכמים' first step seems to make no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: but he does not take it!

phrases.english: As a gift?
But he does not take it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the חכמים' opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חכמים' ruling 'נותנין לו לשום מתנה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case is a poor man who refuses help, so giving him a gift contradicts the case itself.

steps.title: רבא: start by offering it as a gift
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the חכמים mean we first offer it to him as a gift. If he refuses, then we give it as a loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It means to open with him by offering it as a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question. The חכמים do not mean we force a gift on him, only that we first offer it as one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'gift' in the חכמים' view describes the opening offer, not what he must accept. If he will not take a gift, we fall back on giving it as a loan. This removes the contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: to open with him, to begin the offer

steps.whatToRemember: Even a poor man who refuses help must be supported, and we choose the most respectful way to do it, whether as a gift or as a loan.

phrases.english: Rava said:
To open with him by offering it as a gift.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לִפְתּוֹחַ לוֹ לְשׁוּם מַתָּנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by explaining what 'gift' means in the חכמים' view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifying the meaning of the ruling (an opening offer, not a forced gift)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים seemed to say we give a gift to someone who refuses gifts.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים mean we first offer it as a gift; if he refuses, we give it as a loan.

steps.title: Someone who has money but will not use it
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If a person has money but refuses to spend it on himself, the fund gives to him as a gift and later collects it back from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he has money but doesn't want to support himself with it, they give him money as a gift, and later they go back and collect it from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves from the poor man who refuses help to a new case: a man who has money but is too stingy to use it on himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This man is not really poor, so the help is only a gift on the surface. Since he can afford it, the fund will later take the money back.

keyTerms.meaning: He has money of his own

phrases.english: If he has money but does not want to support himself with it,
they give to him as a gift,
and then they go back and collect it from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא from step 17 and gives its second case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who has money but won't use it gets money as a gift, which is later collected back from him.

steps.title: If they collect from him, he will stop taking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the fund collects the money back, he will figure it out and refuse to take anything again.
steps.simpleTranslation: They go back and collect from him? Then he won't take any more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule it just read: collecting the money back seems to ruin the whole plan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of calling it a gift is to get him to accept help. Once he has to pay it back, he will see that it was never a gift and will refuse in the future.

phrases.english: They go back and collect from him?
Then he will not take anymore!

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹזְרִין וְנִפְרָעִין הֵימֶנּוּ, תּוּ לָא שָׁקֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks how the rule in step 20 could work in practice.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the fund collects back from the man who has money
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Collecting back exposes the 'gift' as a loan, so he will stop accepting help.

steps.title: They collect only after he dies
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the fund collects from his estate only after his death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: they collect after his death.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא solves the problem by explaining when the collecting happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While he is alive he never pays anything back, so he keeps accepting. The fund takes its money from what he leaves behind after he dies.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
After his death.
phrases.notes: He means the fund collects from what he leaves behind once he dies.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifies the timing of the collection
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Collection happens during his life, so he would stop taking.
steps.terutzMaskana: Collection happens only from his estate after death, so he keeps taking while alive.

steps.title: רבי שמעון's different approach
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון says the fund does not deal with someone who has money. For a poor man who refuses, they ask for collateral and give a loan, so he keeps his dignity.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: if he has money and won't support himself, we don't get involved with him. If he has no money and won't take צדקה, we tell him: bring collateral and take, so he feels good about himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings רבי שמעון, who disagrees on both cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the man with money, רבי שמעון says the fund has no duty to him at all. For the poor man, a loan with collateral makes him feel he is borrowing like anyone else, not taking a handout.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not get involved with him
So his spirit is lifted, so he feels respected

phrases.english: רבי שמעון says:
If he has money but does not want to support himself,
we do not get involved with him.
If he does not have money and does not want to be supported,
we say to him: bring collateral and take,
so that he will feel good about himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different opinion on both cases of the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No help for someone who has money. For a poor man who refuses, a loan against collateral.

steps.title: רבי יהודה reads the double wording as two cases
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: רבי יהודה learns from 'העבט' the poor man who refuses (loan, then gift), and from 'תעביטנו' the man with money who refuses (gift, collected after death).
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'העבט' is someone who has nothing and won't take support: we give it as a loan and then turn it into a gift. 'תעביטנו' is someone who has money and won't support himself: we give it as a gift and collect it back after his death. These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that finds a source in the Torah for the two cases discussed so far.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the verb twice, 'העבט תעביטנו', and רבי יהודה says each word teaches a separate case. This gives a Torah source for the rules of steps 17 to 22.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall surely lend him', the Torah's double phrase

phrases.english: The רבנן taught:
'Ha'avet' is one who does not have money
and does not want to be supported,
that we give to him as a loan,
and then we turn around and give it to him as a gift.
'Ta'avitenu' is one who has money
and does not want to support himself,
that we give to him as a gift,
and then collect it back from him after his death.
These are the words of רבי יהודה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a Torah source for the two cases from the earlier ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each half of 'העבט תעביטנו' teaches a different refusing person and how to help him.

steps.title: The חכמים: no duty to the man who has money
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say that if someone has money and refuses to use it, the fund does not get involved.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: if he has money and won't support himself, we don't get involved with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the חכמים, who argue with רבי יהודה about the man who has money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the second case, the חכמים have no use for the extra word 'תעביטנו'. That sets up the next question.

phrases.english: And the חכמים say:
If he has money but does not want to support himself,
we do not get involved with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי יהודה's second case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The community has no duty toward someone who has money but won't use it.

steps.title: Then what is 'תעביטנו' for?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks the חכמים: if you don't learn the second case, how do you explain the extra word 'תעביטנו'?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, how do I explain 'תעביטנו'?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges the חכמים, who seem to leave the Torah's extra word with no meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה used each word for a separate case. The חכמים drop the second case, so they must explain why the Torah repeats the word.

keyTerms.meaning: How do I explain, what do I do with

phrases.english: But then how do I explain 'ta'avitenu'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the חכמים of step 25.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every word in the Torah should teach something, and the חכמים leave 'תעביטנו' unused.

steps.title: The Torah speaks the way people speak
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the doubled word is just normal human speech and does not teach a separate law.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah spoke in the language of people.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים answer that the repeated word is simply a normal way of talking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People often double a verb for emphasis. So, according to the חכמים, 'העבט תעביטנו' does not point to a second case.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah spoke in the language of people

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה learns two cases from 'העבט תעביטנו'. The חכמים say the double wording is ordinary speech, so there is no duty toward someone who has money but won't use it.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the חכמים never learn from extra words in the Torah. Here they say this particular repetition is just normal speech.

phrases.english: The Torah spoke in the language of people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the extra word as ordinary speech
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The double word must teach a second case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The repetition is normal speech and teaches no separate law.

steps.title: מר עוקבא's daily secret gift
steps.stepSummary: A story begins: מר עוקבא used to throw four זוזים into a poor neighbor's door slot every day.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר עוקבא had a poor man in his neighborhood. Every day he would throw four זוזים into the slot by the door for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about giving צדקה in a way that protects the poor man's dignity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gift was secret, so the poor man never knew who was helping him. This sets up what happens next in the story.

keyTerms.meaning: The slot by the door's hinge

phrases.english: מר עוקבא had a poor man in his neighborhood,
and he was used to, every day,
throwing four זוזים for him
into the slot by the door's hinge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story on the same subject of respectful צדקה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר עוקבא gave his poor neighbor money in secret every day.

steps.title: The poor man wants to know who it is
steps.stepSummary: One day the poor man decides to find out who is helping him. That day מר עוקבא was late from the בית מדרש, and his wife came with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day he said: I will go and see who is doing me this kindness. That day מר עוקבא was late at the בית מדרש, and his wife came with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story builds tension: the secret might be found out. The גמרא is setting up the next part of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The poor man plans to watch the door, and this time מר עוקבא comes together with his wife. The story will go on to show how they deal with this.

keyTerms.meaning: He was delayed (it got late for him)

phrases.english: One day he said:
phrases.notes: Both bracketed phrases mean 'one day.' Some versions say it in Hebrew (round brackets), and the corrected wording says it in Aramaic (square brackets).

phrases.english: I will go and see
who is doing this kindness for me.
That day it got late
for מר עוקבא at the בית מדרש,
and his wife came with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of step 28 and sets up what happens next.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The poor man plans to find out who his giver is, on the day מר עוקבא and his wife come together.

steps.title: The poor man chases them, and they hide in a hot furnace
steps.stepSummary: The poor man notices the door moving and runs out after them. מר עוקבא and his wife flee into a furnace that is still hot, and מר עוקבא's feet start to burn.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they saw someone moving the door, the poor man went out after them. They ran away from him and went into a furnace whose fire had been raked out. מר עוקבא's feet were getting burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The story keeps going. The poor man tries to catch his helper, so מר עוקבא and his wife run and hide in a hot furnace rather than be seen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger is real, because the coals are still hot enough to burn his feet. The story is building toward the question of why they would risk getting hurt just to stay hidden.

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּחַזְיֵוהּ דְּקָא מַצְלֵי לֵיהּ לְדַשָּׁא,
phrases.english: When they saw that someone was turning the door,
phrases.notes: This is the moment the coins come through the door slot, and the poor man finally notices.

phrases.english: he went out after them.
They ran away from before him,
they went into a certain furnace
whose fire had been raked out,
phrases.notes: The fire itself was cleared out, but the furnace was still hot.

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה קָא מִיקַּלְיָין כַּרְעֵיהּ דְּמָר עוּקְבָא.
phrases.english: and מר עוקבא's feet were getting burned.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּחַזְיֵוהּ דְּקָא מַצְלֵי לֵיהּ לְדַשָּׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from step 29, where the poor man decided to find out who was helping him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר עוקבא and his wife hide in a hot furnace so the poor man will not discover them.

steps.title: His wife's feet are not burned, and she explains why
steps.stepSummary: His wife tells him to rest his feet on hers. He is upset that her merit seems greater, and she explains that her צדקה helps the poor more directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: His wife said to him: Lift your feet and put them on my feet. He felt bad. She said to him: I am at home, and my help reaches the poor right away.
steps.whatsHappening: His wife's feet are protected while his are burning. She explains that her kind of giving is more immediate than his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר עוקבא is upset because her protection shows that her merit is greater than his. She explains that she is at home and hands out help that the poor person can use right away, while his money still has to be turned into what the poor person needs.

keyTerms.meaning: his wife (literally, 'the one of his house')

phrases.english: His wife said to him:
Lift your feet and put them on my feet.
He felt bad.
phrases.notes: He realized her feet weren't burning, which meant her merit was greater than his.

phrases.english: She said to him:
I am found inside the house,
and my help is close at hand.
phrases.notes: She means that what she gives can be used right away, while money still has to be spent on what the poor person needs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the furnace scene and explains why the wife was protected.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: צדקה that brings the poor person immediate help carries greater merit.

steps.title: Why go to such extremes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why מר עוקבא and his wife risked a burning furnace just to stay hidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why all this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses the story to ask a question. This sets up the next step, which explains their behavior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jumping into a hot furnace seems extreme and even dangerous. The גמרא wants a source that justifies going that far to avoid being seen by the poor man.

keyTerms.meaning: all this, to such a degree

phrases.english: And why all this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the behavior described in the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why did they put themselves in danger rather than be discovered?

steps.title: Better to enter a fire than to shame someone in public
steps.stepSummary: Several chains of names report one teaching: a person should throw himself into a fiery furnace rather than embarrass someone in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: As מר זוטרא בר טוביה said in the name of רב, and some say רב הונא בר ביזנא said in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא, and some say רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: It is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to embarrass his friend in public.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Embarrassing someone in public is so serious that a person should be ready to go into fire to avoid it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the poor man had caught them, he would have been embarrassed to face the people supporting him. Their jump into the furnace is this teaching acted out in real life.

keyTerms.meaning: make someone's face go white, meaning embarrass him

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: As Mar Zutra bar Toviya said in the name of Rav,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר בִּיזְנָא
phrases.english: and some say Rav Huna bar Bizna said
in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לָהּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
It is better for a person
to throw himself into a fiery furnace
than to whiten his friend's face in public.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 32 with a known teaching.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Shaming someone in public is so severe that it is better to enter a furnace than to do it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the famous source for how seriously the תורה treats embarrassing another person.

steps.title: The source: תמר
steps.stepSummary: The teaching is learned from תמר, who was ready to be burned rather than publicly name יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this? From תמר, as it is written: 'She was being taken out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the פסוק behind the teaching. תמר was being taken out to be burned, and she still did not openly shame יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תמר only hinted to יהודה in private, so he could admit the truth on his own. She was willing to die rather than embarrass him publicly, and this is the model for the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: from where do we know this?
she was being taken out (to be burned)

phrases.english: From where do we know this?
From Tamar,
as it is written: "She was being taken out."
phrases.notes: בראשית 38:25. Even while being taken out to be burned, she sent a private hint to יהודה instead of naming him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the scriptural source for the teaching in step 33.
steps.raayaObject: Better to enter fire than to shame someone in public
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of תמר in בראשית 38
steps.whatToRemember: מר עוקבא and his wife hid in a hot furnace because it is better to be burned than to embarrass someone in public, as we learn from תמר.

steps.title: A new story: מר עוקבא's yearly gift before יום כיפור
steps.stepSummary: מר עוקבא used to send 400 זוזים to a poor neighbor every year on ערב יום כיפור.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר עוקבא had a poor man in his neighborhood to whom he used to send four hundred זוזים every ערב יום כיפור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a second story about מר עוקבא's צדקה. This line sets up the background.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a large yearly gift to one regular recipient. The background prepares us for what happens one year when his son delivers it.

phrases.english: Mar Ukva had a poor man in his neighborhood
to whom he used to send
four hundred zuz
every eve of Yom Kippur.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about מר עוקבא's צדקה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר עוקבא gave a fixed yearly gift to a poor neighbor.

steps.title: The son reports that the poor man lives in luxury
steps.stepSummary: His son brings the money and comes back saying the poor man does not need it, because he saw them sprinkling old wine for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day he sent it through his son. The son came back and said: He doesn't need it. מר עוקבא asked: What did you see? He said: I saw them sprinkling old wine for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The son thinks the poor man is not really poor, because he saw him enjoying a luxury. This sets up מר עוקבא's surprising reaction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Old wine was expensive, and sprinkling it just for its smell looks wasteful. The son concludes that the man does not deserve צדקה.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד שַׁדְּרִינְהוּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ בְּיַד בְּרֵיהּ.
phrases.english: One day he sent them to him through his son.
The son came back and said to him: He doesn't need it.
He said: What did you see?

phrases.aramaic: חֲזַאי דְּקָא מְזַלְּפִי לֵיהּ יַיִן יָשָׁן.
phrases.english: I saw them sprinkling old wine for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד שַׁדְּרִינְהוּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ בְּיַד בְּרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the second story with the son's report.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son thinks a poor man who enjoys luxury does not need צדקה.

steps.title: מר עוקבא doubles the gift
steps.stepSummary: מר עוקבא says that if the man is so used to luxury, he needs even more, so he doubles the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: He is that pampered? He doubled the money and sent it to him.
steps.whatsHappening: Instead of cutting the gift, מר עוקבא doubles it. This is the high point of the second story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר עוקבא sees it the opposite way from his son. A man who grew up with luxury really needs more to live in the way he is used to, so he deserves a bigger gift.

phrases.english: He said: He is that pampered!
He doubled them and sent them to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: מר עוקבא reacts to his son's report.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A poor person used to luxury is given according to what he is used to, even more.

steps.title: On his deathbed, מר עוקבא gives away half his money
steps.stepSummary: As he is dying, מר עוקבא checks his צדקה records and finds 7,000 gold דינרים. He feels it is too little and gives away half of his wealth.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he was dying, he said: Bring me my צדקה records. He found 7,000 gold דינרים written there. He said: My supplies are light and the road is long. He got up and gave away half his money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a third story about מר עוקבא. Even a huge amount of צדקה feels too small to him for the long journey ahead, so he gives half his money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'road' is the journey to the next world, and the 'supplies' are his מצוות. Giving away half his money will clash with a known rule, which sets up the next step's question.

keyTerms.meaning: he was dying (literally, 'his soul was resting')

phrases.english: When he was dying,
he said: Bring me my charity records.
He found written in it
seven thousand gold dinars.
He said: My supplies are light, and the road is long.
phrases.notes: He means his מצוות are not enough for the long journey to the next world.

phrases.english: He got up and gave away half his money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about מר עוקבא, at the end of his life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר עוקבא gave away half of his wealth before dying.

steps.title: Isn't giving more than a fifth forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges מר עוקבא's act, citing the rule made in אושא that a person should not give away more than one-fifth of his money.
steps.simpleTranslation: How could he do this? Didn't רבי אילעאי say: In אושא they made a rule that one who gives freely should not give more than a fifth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the story with a known rule. Giving away half seems to break the limit of one-fifth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule from אושא puts a ceiling on how much צדקה a person gives. A great man like מר עוקבא giving half his money looks like a direct contradiction of that rule.

keyTerms.meaning: אושא, the town where the חכמים made several rules

phrases.english: How could he do this?
But didn't Rabbi Ilai say:
In Usha they made a rule:
One who gives freely should not give more than a fifth!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי עֲבַד הָכִי וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אִילְעַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the deathbed act in step 38.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר עוקבא giving away half his money
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule from אושא forbids giving more than one-fifth, so giving half should not be allowed.

steps.title: The one-fifth limit applies only during a person's life
steps.stepSummary: The limit exists so a person does not become poor himself. After death that worry no longer applies, so there is no problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule applies during a person's lifetime, because he might lose his wealth. But after death we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The one-fifth rule protects a living person, and someone giving at the end of his life has no such concern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason for the rule defines its scope: a living person who gives too much could become poor himself. Once he is dying, that reason is gone, so מר עוקבא was allowed to give half.

keyTerms.meaning: these words apply (only in this case)
he will lose his property and become poor
we have no problem with it

phrases.english: These words apply during his lifetime,
because he might lose his wealth.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לְאַחַר מִיתָה לֵית לַן בַּהּ.
phrases.english: But after death, we have no problem with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 39.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule to the case its reason covers
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The one-fifth limit applies always, so מר עוקבא's gift was improper.
steps.terutzMaskana: The limit applies only during life, because of the fear of becoming poor. Giving at death is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule from אושא limits צדקה to one-fifth so a person won't become poor himself. When giving at the time of death, more than one-fifth is allowed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical הלכה that the one-fifth ceiling does not apply to what a person gives away at the end of his life.

steps.title: רבי אבא gives coins without the poor having to face him
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא tied coins in his scarf, tossed it behind him near the homes of the poor, and kept an eye out for cheats.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא would tie coins in his scarf and throw it behind him. He would place himself near the homes of the poor, and he would turn his eyes to guard the money from swindlers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells another צדקה story, this time about how רבי אבא gave money in a hidden way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Throwing the money behind him meant the poor person could take it without facing the giver, so no one was embarrassed. He still glanced sideways just enough to make sure cheats did not grab money meant for real poor people. He cared both about the poor person's dignity and about the money reaching the right hands.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אַבָּא הֲוָה צָיַיר זוּזֵי בְּסוּדָרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba would tie coins in his scarf,
and throw it behind him,
and he would place himself near the homes of the poor,
and he would turn his eyes to watch out for swindlers.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַבָּא הֲוָה צָיַיר זוּזֵי בְּסוּדָרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the מר עוקבא stories, the גמרא brings a new צדקה story about a different חכם.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אבא gave צדקה in a hidden way to protect the dignity of the poor, while still guarding the money from cheats.

steps.title: רבי חנינא's wife reports that the poor man does not need the money
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא sent a poor man four זוזים every ערב שבת. One time he sent it with his wife, and she came back saying the man doesn't need it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא had a certain poor man to whom he used to send four זוזים every ערב שבת. One day he sent the money with his wife. She came back and said to him: He doesn't need it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about רבי חנינא and sets up a surprise: his wife says the poor man is not really poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a regular, weekly gift, so it was a set arrangement. The twist is the wife's claim that the man doesn't need it, which raises the question of whether the gift should continue. The next lines will show why she thought so.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina had a certain poor man
to whom he was used to sending
four zuz every Shabbat eve.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד שַׁדְּרִינְהוּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ בְּיַד דְּבֵיתְהוּ,
phrases.english: One day he sent them to him in the hand of his wife,
she came back and said to him: He doesn't need it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another צדקה story, similar in shape to the מר עוקבא story, where the messenger reports that the poor man doesn't need the money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי חנינא's wife reports that the poor man he supports does not need צדקה.

steps.title: רבי חנינא asks his wife what she saw
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא asks his wife what made her think the poor man doesn't need the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did you see?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא asks his wife for the reason behind her claim. This sets up her answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא does not simply stop giving; he first wants to know what she saw. This prepares the next step, where she describes what she overheard.

phrases.english: What did you see?
phrases.notes: רבי חנינא is asking his wife why she said the man doesn't need it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the wife's claim in the previous step.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What evidence made the wife decide the poor man does not need צדקה?

steps.title: The wife begins describing what she overheard
steps.stepSummary: She says she heard people inside the house asking the poor man what he dines with. Her report continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: I heard them saying to him: With what do you dine:
steps.whatsHappening: The wife starts to answer, telling רבי חנינא about a conversation she overheard in the poor man's house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She is explaining why she thinks he does not need צדקה: the household's question suggests he lives in a fancy way. Her sentence finishes on the next amud, where we learn what choice they offered him.

phrases.english: I heard them saying to him:
With what do you dine:
phrases.notes: Her report isn't finished; it continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי חנינא's question by starting to describe what she overheard.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: She overheard the household asking the poor man what he dines with. This begins her evidence that he lives in luxury, and her explanation continues afterward.
